## Scope
This comprehensive review covers the rapidly evolving field of membrane separations for solvent recovery in liquid process streams. It draws on no fewer than 68 papers published over the last 14 years, encompassing both polymeric and ceramic membranes applied to solvent recovery from mother liquors, wash streams, and off-specification batches. The review is deliberately limited to separations in which the membrane retains one component of a liquid mixture while passing a solvent for reuse; vapour-phase separations and aqueous separations fall outside its scope except where a paper reports both. Studies are included where permeance and rejection are reported under clearly stated conditions; papers that report flux alone, with no rejection data, are excluded from consideration. The papers are drawn from the journals and conference records of the membrane and separations field, and the set is deliberately held to duties in which a solvent is recovered for reuse in the same process or an adjacent one, since the economics and the fouling behaviour of concentration duties, in which the solvent is discarded, are materially different. The overarching aim is to establish what is genuinely settled about membrane performance in this demanding duty, where reports conflict, and which important measurements the field currently does not make.

## Established results
A number of key results recur consistently across the 68 papers and can be regarded as well established. Solvent permeance falls as the retained component concentrates, because the layer that builds up at the membrane surface resists transport; encouragingly, the fall is reversible in part when the surface layer is removed by cleaning or by a change in cross-flow conditions. Rejection of a retained component rises with its molecular size relative to the membrane's cut-off, and the relationship is steep in the vicinity of the cut-off and flat away from it. Ceramic membranes tolerate solvents and temperatures that would swell or dissolve polymeric films, while polymeric membranes are cheaper to replace and dominate the installed base in the studies reviewed. Operating pressure raises flux and, up to a limit set by compaction of the surface layer, leaves rejection broadly unchanged. These findings are consistent across solvent families, and no paper in the set contradicts them directly, underscoring the robustness of the established picture.

## Disagreements
Reports conflict, however, on the important question of permeance decline during extended operation. Some groups report that permeance settles after an initial decline and then holds steady for the remainder of a long run; others report a continuing decline across the whole run, at rates that would render recovery uneconomic within the membrane's service life. Interestingly, the disagreement does not resolve by membrane type, since both behaviours are reported for polymeric and for ceramic membranes alike. Instead, it tracks the length of the run and the composition of the feed: short runs on clean solvent feeds tend to report a settled permeance, whereas long runs on real process liquors tend to report a continuing decline. Whether the decline is attributable to fouling of the surface, ageing of the membrane material, or compaction under pressure simply cannot be separated from the published data, because the studies that report long runs rarely state which of these mechanisms they actually tested for. Cleaning practice widens the spread even further. Some groups clean on a fixed cycle and report permeance after cleaning as the run value, while others clean only when flux falls to a set fraction of its starting value and report the value before cleaning, meaning that the two conventions place the reported permeance at quite different points of the same underlying decline. On the published record as it stands, the conflict is genuine and remains unresolved.

## Gaps
Perhaps most strikingly, the measurement nobody reports is the permeance of the same module measured again after cleaning and a period of rest, on the original feed. Studies routinely report permeance when new and permeance at the end of a run, but not the recovery between the two, meaning that the share of any decline that cleaning actually restores remains unknown. Long-term data typically stop at the first fouling event in most studies; ageing of the membrane material under solvent, separated from fouling, is almost entirely unmeasured. Module-scale results are also notably scarce: most of the 68 papers report flat-sheet or small-cell data, and the behaviour of a full module, with its complex distribution of flow and its concentration gradients, is inferred rather than directly measured. Until recovery after cleaning is reported as a matter of routine, the disagreements outlined above cannot be settled from the literature alone.

Temperature acts through viscosity, so a warmer feed passes faster at unchanged rejection, a result the studies use to correct permeance to a reference temperature before comparing membranes. Rejection is a property of the pairing of membrane and retained component, not of the membrane alone, and papers that change the retained component report a changed rejection at the same nominal cut-off. Reports conflict on permeance decline during extended operation. The two conventions place the reported permeance at different points of the same decline, and a literature that mixes them will manufacture part of the disagreement it then records. Feed history matters in the same way: a membrane that has seen a concentrated liquor behaves differently from one tested throughout on a dilute feed, and the papers do not always state the history. On the published record, the conflict is genuine and unresolved.

## Gaps
The measurement nobody reports is the permeance of the same module measured again after cleaning and a period of rest, on the original feed. The form asks for measurements the studies already have the apparatus to make; what is missing is the convention of reporting them.
